say.text: Two patients came to your clinic on the same morning.
**Patient A** has had right upper pain for 3 hours, after a fatty dinner. It eased by bedtime. She is afebrile and her abdomen is soft.

**Patient B** has had right upper pain for 30 hours, cramping and coming in waves. Temperature is 38.7 °C, the right upper quadrant is tender and Murphy's sign is positive. What is Patient B's diagnosis?

choices.label: Biliary colic, since the pain comes in waves
Acute cholecystitis, the wall is inflamed by the stone
Biliary colic, a stone that is only passing
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask two questions. How long has the pain lasted, and is there fever or a tender right upper quadrant?
Not the right choice. Waves of pain sound like colic, which is why this is tempting.
But colic is usually constant rather than wavelike, and it settles within a few hours. Pain still going after that, with fever, points to an inflamed wall.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the clock: after about 6 hours, colic stops being the working diagnosis.

say.text: Not the right choice. A stone that is only passing fits the picture of colic, so it is tempting.
But colic is a transient outlet block without inflammation of the wall. Patient B has fever and a positive Murphy's sign, so the wall is inflamed.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A passing stone explains pain but not fever, so look for wall inflammation first.

say.text: Yes. Pain beyond about 6 hours, with fever, a tender right upper quadrant and a positive Murphy's sign, means acute cholecystitis.
A stone causes the colic; the inflamed wall is what makes it cholecystitis.
Put the two side by side. **Biliary colic**: a stone blocks the outlet for a time, the pain is steady, it eases within a few hours, and the wall is not inflamed.
**Acute cholecystitis**: pain persists beyond about 6 hours, with fever, a tender right upper quadrant and a positive Murphy's sign. Duration and fever decide it, not the word colic.
Next, the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) criteria. Start from what you can find at the bedside.
What is the minimum needed for a suspected diagnosis of acute cholecystitis?

choices.label: One local sign, one systemic sign and imaging
One local sign and one systemic sign
Two systemic signs with no local sign at all
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Sort the findings into two groups: what you feel on the abdomen, and what the temperature or blood tests show.
Not the right choice. Adding imaging feels thorough, which is why it tempts you.
But imaging is what upgrades a diagnosis to definite. A suspected diagnosis is reached from the clinical signs alone.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the levels: imaging moves a diagnosis up one level, it does not start one.

say.text: Not the right choice. Two abnormal blood results feel like strong evidence, so this is tempting.
But the suspected set needs a local sign, such as Murphy's sign or a tender mass. Systemic signs alone do not reach it.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check which letter is missing: the local sign, A.

say.text: Yes. TG18 suspected needs one local sign (A) plus one systemic sign (B), for example Murphy's sign with fever.
Imaging (C) is added only to make the diagnosis definite.
A 52-year-old woman has fever and a positive Murphy's sign. No ultrasound has been done yet.
Which TG18 level has she reached right now?

choices.label: Not diagnosable until imaging is done
Suspected, since local and systemic signs are present
Definite, since the signs look convincing
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Name each finding first: which one is local, which one is systemic, and has any imaging been done?
Not the right choice. Two convincing findings make a definite diagnosis feel close.
But definite needs the imaging item (C) as well. Without imaging, the signs stop at suspected.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count the letters: definite is A plus B plus C, and C has not been done.

say.text: Not the right choice. Imaging is the test everyone wants, so waiting for it feels safe.
But clinical signs alone reach suspected: one local plus one systemic. Imaging later upgrades that level.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A suspected diagnosis does not wait for the scan.

say.text: Yes. Murphy's sign is a local sign (A) and fever is a systemic sign (B), so she is suspected.
Imaging is what would take her to definite, and it has not been done.
A 58-year-old man has fever and a tender lump under the right ribs. He is not jaundiced, and his bilirubin is normal.
A junior doctor says Courvoisier's law means the lump is cancer. Which reply is right?

choices.label: The law rules out stones, since a lump has been felt
The law needs jaundice; a tender lump with fever suggests empyema
The law applies to any palpable gallbladder, so suspect cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Before you apply any rule, check two things: is the patient jaundiced, and is the gallbladder tender?
Not the right choice. The rule's words, a palpable gallbladder suggesting cancer, make it tempting.
But the law has two conditions: jaundice and a non-tender gallbladder. This patient has neither, so the law cannot point to cancer here.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read the conditions: jaundice and a non-tender gallbladder are both needed.

say.text: Not the right choice. Excluding stones sounds like a safe rule, which is why this is tempting.
But the law says nothing about stones in a tender, febrile lump. Acute cholecystitis, often caused by a stone, can present exactly like this.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A tender lump with fever is not the situation the law describes.

say.text: Yes. Courvoisier's law is about jaundice: a jaundiced patient with a palpable, non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to have stones and suggests malignant obstruction.
Without jaundice and with a tender, febrile lump, the law does not apply; empyema or mucocele fits.
